Record stable provider/model identifiers, an observed revision where available, display aliases, supported modalities, tool/structured-output support, input/output context limits, prices with currency and timestamp, credential reference, endpoint/deployment identity, locality/privacy policy, quotas and last useful probe. Keep declared capabilities, observed capabilities and the actual effective invocation separate. If a provider exposes only a moving alias, record that limitation; do not invent an immutable revision.

A newly registered model may be visible before it is eligible. An unsupported operation gets a precise reason: missing tool use, insufficient context, unapproved egress, unavailable credential or unknown price under a strict cost ceiling. General text-only inference remains possible through the plain inference adapter, even when Pi cannot use that model as a coding worker.

### Initial policy: deterministic, inspectable and free of routing tokens

1. Read the task class and constraints from structured intake. The operator or existing liaison can supply them; a separate LLM classifier is optional and charged to the task.
2. Filter by capabilities, locality, credentials, current resource availability, budget and operational health.
3. Select an eligible named profile using explicit rules and a measured per-class preference table. Begin with curated preferences where there are no outcomes, and label them provisional.
4. Prefer the cheapest candidate that meets the class's quality requirement. If evidence cannot distinguish candidates, use the configured baseline or stable tie-break and report the uncertainty; a tied score need not stall routine work.
5. Reserve the attempt budget, record the reason and effective configuration, then dispatch. Retry/fallback stays within the same original constraints and remaining budget.

Avoid one global weighted score combining privacy, quality, speed and cost. Privacy is a constraint; cost and latency are objectives after eligibility and the quality requirement. HEE's existing 40/25/20/15 weighting can be kept as an experimental comparator, not silently called optimal. [Existing weights](sources/C06.rs).

Initial profiles might be `quick-text`, `routine-code`, `deep-debug`, `review`, and `private-local`. These are task policies, not permanent model names. Populate their model IDs from the accounts and runtimes actually available at commissioning. `deep-debug` may route directly to a stronger model when a cheap first attempt would merely add delay. `private-local` must never fall back to a remote endpoint without a changed task constraint.

### Learning which choices work

Every completed attempt records task class, repository context, recipe/version, queue/runtime, input/output/cache/reasoning usage when reported, tool and verification cost, acceptance result and human rework. Count failed, cancelled and abandoned attempts; cost per accepted task includes them. Distinguish deterministic acceptance from reviewer judgment. A model reviewing its own work is not an independent ground truth.

Use a small, frozen set of representative tasks: documentation, contained code edits, debugging, testing, and a privacy-constrained case. Include hard negatives and tasks where existing tests are insufficient. Compare candidate profiles with the current fixed-model baseline and the simple routing policy using matched tasks and the same acceptance procedure. Split tuning tasks from held-out tasks; refresh for drift without rewriting historical outcomes.

Promotion requires a meaningful cost or completion-time improvement at acceptable quality, with uncertainty reported by class. Do not impose HEE's 50-case/100-execution baseline as a universal statistical guarantee. Required sample size depends on effect size, variance and harm from a bad choice. Where the evidence is thin, keep the baseline. Learned routers, contextual bandits and model-as-router calls are later candidates only if their net savings exceed their own cost and maintenance.

A route explanation should fit one screen: chosen recipe, hard exclusions, preference basis, estimated cost, fallback and evidence freshness. Full model transcripts are not necessary to understand why the route was chosen.

sections.title: Agent and service rosters that reflect reality
sections.body:
### Agent roster

Separate an **agent profile** from a running **agent instance**. A profile is a reusable recipe: role, harness, allowed models/tools, context sources, limits and acceptance expectations. An instance has a task attempt, process/session identity, generation, workspace, start time, current lease, observed state and usage. A Herdr pane is a presentation attachment, not the agent's identity.

Use small lifecycle vocabularies. Profiles can be draft, available, disabled or retired. Instances can be starting, ready, busy, waiting, stopping, exited or unknown. Keep the last observation and its age. Do not interpret a successful spawn, open pane, old status file or surviving shell as readiness. Registering a profile never starts an agent.

An initial roster needs add/update/list/inspect/disable, capability refresh, and a concise explanation when a profile cannot run a task. Credentials are references to separately managed secrets; they never appear in roster exports. Retain instance histories after retirement so failures and costs remain attributable.

### Service roster

“Binary, daemon, library, neural operator” combines packaging, lifecycle and function. Model those as separate axes instead of one expanding enum:

| Axis | Examples | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Artifact | Binary, library, container image, model weights, script, schema | Version, source and installation identity |
| Runtime | One-shot process, daemon, in-process library, remote endpoint, batch job | Appropriate lifecycle and health operations |
| Role | Model server, compiler, indexer, verifier, router, neural operator, backup | What capability a task can request |
| Owner | systemd user unit, Podman Quadlet, calling process, remote provider, human | Who may start, stop, update or repair it |

Each service record includes ID, version/digest where available, capability inputs/outputs, dependencies, resource claims, endpoint or invocation, lifecycle owner, desired state, observed state, useful-health probe, probe freshness, restart policy, data paths and recovery notes. SQLite owns admitted roster record revisions, effective selections, observed state and history. TOML supplies reviewed bootstrap/import/export manifests; editing a file alone has no effect on admitted authority. Static coordinator startup settings may remain authoritative TOML configuration. An imported inventory is an observation with a timestamp, not a permanent assertion of health.

A library has no independent PID or restart action; validate its consumer and compatibility. A neural operator needs an input/output contract, model/artifact identity, shapes/dtypes/units where relevant, supported domain, resource needs and a numerical/reference check. Register its serving daemon separately when one exists. This handles scientific operators without forcing them into LLM semantics or inventing a new supervisor.

Start with inspect-only discovery of a small set of user services. Add lifecycle actions only for explicitly managed entries. Service management must not take over arbitrary existing units just because they were discovered. Changes go through the established owner, with dependency checks and a result readback.

Useful additional catalogues are repositories/workspaces, tools and their required services, accepted artifacts, task acceptance procedures, and model deployments. Implement these as small typed tables/views within the same registry, not separate roster daemons. Defer a universal ontology, semantic graph and plugin marketplace until there are actual consumers.

Roster creation, mutation and manifest import use the same operator-only `roster.update` boundary: expected-absent creates or expected-revision updates, validated fields and an idempotency key. Invalid or stale imports leave effective records unchanged. Restart cannot re-enable a disabled record from an old file. Export is a snapshot, not a second state owner; active attempts keep their admitted record versions.

sections.title: The closed loop: verification and proof of completion
sections.body:
The control loop is a first-class product contract: **plan → execute → observe → verify → repair or escalate → verify again → close with evidence**. Rust owns the durable transitions; workers produce candidate artifacts; verifiers supply scoped observations; Julia evaluates outcomes across runs. The loop is event-driven and quiet while waiting. A loop is not an instruction to keep agents perpetually active.

### One bounded loop record, three useful scopes

Every task records its objective and acceptance revision, input/workspace identity, current iteration, remaining budget/deadline, active attempt and verifier, evidence references, and next permitted transition. Persist the transition and outbox event together so a restart resumes the recorded obligation. Do not create a second loop database or a separate orchestration daemon.

| Scope | Loop and owner | Closure condition |
|---|---|---|
| Individual task | Rust dispatches a worker, checks its artifact, and issues a bounded repair request | All mandatory criteria pass on the actual candidate, with required review and a committed completion record |
| Cohort / workflow | Integrator joins dependent outputs, verifies the assembled result, and assigns specific integration repairs | Parent criteria pass; completed child tasks alone cannot close the parent |
| Operational learning | Julia compares accepted outcomes and failures; maintainer considers a policy candidate; Rust performs scoped promotion/rollback | A declared comparison supports the change; learning cannot alter an active task's acceptance or authority |

### Verification drives the next action

Before execution, specify each acceptance criterion, verifier kind, required inputs and expected evidence. Use deterministic checks for machine-testable properties, review for judgment, and explicit owner acceptance where the outcome requires it. Do not add an LLM reviewer to every inexpensive deterministic operation. Verification effort and any model calls consume the same task budget, with an allowance reserved so execution cannot routinely spend everything before checking.

After execution, freeze or identify the candidate content and verify that exact artifact in the intended environment. A Git commit alone is insufficient when relevant tracked modifications or untracked inputs exist; bind the relevant content/configuration and dependencies actually checked. Prevent concurrent mutation during the decisive check, or reject the result if the subject changed. A later edit invalidates affected checks; unchanged, demonstrably independent evidence can be reused. Do not mandate unrelated full-suite reruns for cosmetic changes.

| Verification outcome | Recorded action |
|---|---|
| Every mandatory criterion passes | Validate the evidence bundle, commit accepted status and completion event together |
| A criterion fails and repair is feasible within scope/budget | Record the counterexample; dispatch a focused next attempt; rerun affected checks and required regression checks |
| Verifier crashes, times out, checks the wrong subject or has invalid fixtures | Record verification error/unknown; repair the instrument or use an authorised alternative; do not claim an artifact pass or blindly rewrite it |
| Same failure repeats, progress stops, or budget/deadline is exhausted | Stop automatic iteration; record the exhaustion/no-progress reason and request disposition when necessary |
| Input, permission or an external result is missing | Enter waiting with an explicit unblock condition; keep costs quiet |
| Cancellation or unresolved effect occurs | Preserve partial output and uncertainty; confirm owned-process cleanup separately from task success |

Repair requests carry the failing criterion, concrete evidence and permitted change scope, not the entire swarm transcript. Fallback to another model preserves the original privacy, ownership, budget and acceptance requirements. Never silently weaken criteria to make the loop converge. A legitimate change creates a new acceptance revision with the source of authority recorded. A critic's numerical score is advisory unless a previously specified and calibrated criterion actually uses it.

### A minimal proof-of-completion record

“Proof” here means inspectable evidence for explicitly scoped claims, not a mathematical guarantee that arbitrary software is correct. Store one compact completion manifest with references to retained evidence, not a new cryptographic protocol or dozens of closure documents:

- Task ID, acceptance revision, final attempt/generation and loop count.
- Input and candidate identity, relevant environment/configuration, and output/artifact references with content digests.
- Each mandatory criterion mapped to its verifier/version, observation, pass/fail/unknown outcome, timestamp and raw evidence reference; identify actual self-check versus independent review.
- Whole-task usage/cost mode, retries and verification cost; unresolved limitations and explicitly accepted scope exclusions.
- Required reviewer/owner disposition and a preallocated completion event ID. Write the immutable manifest before atomically committing acceptance, its digest/reference and the outbox event. The ledger establishes commit; mutable delivery receipts live in separate records linked by that event ID, so later acknowledgements never rewrite accepted evidence.

The completion predicate is explicit: the current candidate is the verified subject; every mandatory criterion has valid passing evidence; all required dependencies and dispositions are satisfied; the attempt still owns acceptance rights; and no unresolved effect contradicts the completion claim. Missing, stale, skipped or unreadable evidence is not passing evidence. Only the coordinator commits acceptance; workers cannot write the accepted state or manufacture verifier records in its ledger. A hash binds bytes, not the truth of a test or the trustworthiness of a compromised producer.

Final outcome delivery is another observable edge. If the operator notification is lost, retry the notification through the outbox; do not rerun accepted work. Conversely, receiving a “done” message does not accept work. The task view must expose the result, criterion-to-evidence mapping, limitations and delivery state without requiring an LLM to interpret logs.

### Prove the loop itself before release

The first vertical slice must show one deliberately failing candidate repaired and reverified to acceptance, plus an unrepairable or exhausted task stopping truthfully. Crash fixtures cover candidate produced before verification, verifier returned before evidence commit, acceptance committed before notification, and restart during repair. Additional cases cover fabricated worker success, wrong-tree/stale evidence, candidate mutation during checking, verifier failure, repeated non-progress and a successful cohort whose assembled artifact fails. Confirm each producer-to-consumer edge actually carries the intended event; a healthy endpoint or implemented handler alone does not close the wire. These cases directly address the historical ORAC/Zellij gaps. [Dark completion path](sources/D15.md), [SSD wiring map](sources/S01.md), [swarm callback shortcuts](sources/S15.rs), [verifier instrument failures](sources/S05.md).

The same discipline applies to this planning deliverable: requirement coverage, source provenance and artifact checks support a completed planning review. Proposed engine validators remain unavailable and all implementation tasks remain idle. Planning-artifact checks cannot certify the engine, its model performance or a deployment.

### Artifact publication and later readback

Immutable evidence must be published crash-durably under the declared filesystem contract before acceptance commits its digest/reference in SQLite. Completed writes alone do not establish this: qualify file and metadata synchronisation and atomic publication for the actual storage boundary. Retention explicitly protects unresolved obligations and required accepted proof. If evidence later becomes missing, expired or corrupt, preserve the historical acceptance event, disclose current evidence unavailability and never present that history as a fresh verification.

sections.title: Task execution, persistence and recovery
sections.body:
The minimal task record contains ID, intent, task class, repository/workspace, constraints, budget, acceptance procedure, requested route override and dependencies. A task attempt adds recipe identity, lease generation, effective invocation, status, output references and usage. Stable IDs connect these records to a worker conversation and optional Herdr pane.

Proposed task states are queued, running, waiting, checking, accepted, failed and cancelled. Task outcome, attempt execution, effect certainty, cancellation cleanup, verification and notification delivery are separate state dimensions. A cancellation request is nonterminal until required cleanup/effect reconciliation; cancellation and acceptance compete through one atomic terminal transition. Keep retryable attempts beneath the task rather than resetting history. A waiting task records what it is waiting for and who can unblock it. Worker termination moves the task to checking or failed; acceptance is a separate result.

Use SQLite transactions for the task row, attempt row and event/outbox entry together. A unique request/idempotency key prevents duplicate submission; a generation check prevents a stale worker from committing a result after reassignment. The coordinator has one write-owning service, with read queries available through its API. No second JSON file becomes an alternative authoritative task state.

Keep artifacts outside the database by path/content digest and write them before committing a reference to a complete artifact. Keep detailed worker conversation storage in its own runtime; the engine stores references and a short result. An outbox records notifications still to deliver. Duplicate delivery is allowed and deduplicated by event ID.

Persist dispatch intent before launching. A crash between launch and acknowledgement is an ambiguous attempt: reconcile the unit/process/session identity before deciding to retry. There is no general exactly-once guarantee across a provider API and a local database. Do not re-run an edit, publish or external write merely because its response was lost. Read back the outcome where possible; otherwise record uncertainty and request disposition at that point.

On restart, reconcile active attempts, leases, worker state and pending notifications. Use generation and OS process identity, not PID alone. An unprovable worker becomes unknown and does not regain write ownership automatically. Resume a session only if its workspace and intended attempt still match. Never silently resume an old consent or treat a stored terminal transcript as a live process.

A database lease fences ledger commits; it cannot stop an already running process from writing files or calling an external API. Before reassigning the same writable workspace, confirm termination or use a separate isolated attempt workspace and accept its artifacts through the coordinator. Keep an ambiguous old workspace quarantined from integration. External effects require their own idempotency/readback contract. Do not advertise workspace exclusivity merely because a lease expired.

Cancellation has two steps: ask the adapter to stop and observe completion; then terminate the owned process group/container if it exceeds its configured cleanup deadline. Report incomplete cleanup. For the inspected Pi protocol, clear queued follow-ups when cancelling the task because abort can otherwise leave queued work to continue. The adapter must account for retries and compaction calls rather than judging only the first end event. [Pi RPC](sources/A11.md).

Database migrations are versioned and tested forward with a documented rollback policy. Backups use a consistent SQLite backup/checkpoint procedure, not an arbitrary copy of a live main file that omits WAL state. A restore drill must recover task and artifact references on a disposable path. Local checksums detect accidental drift; they do not prove resistance to a compromised user account.

sections.title: Rust, Julia, PyTorch and neural operators
sections.body:
Rust and Julia are fixed product-language requirements. Rust owns task admission, rosters, scheduling, leases, process control, budgets and persistence. Julia owns statistical evaluation, workload analysis, coordination experiments and numerical models. This is a functional split: Julia contributes useful analysis in the first release rather than appearing as a ceremonial second verifier.

### The smallest useful Rust–Julia boundary

The Rust service exports an immutable, schema-versioned dataset of attempts and outcomes. An on-demand Julia process computes per-class acceptance/cost distributions, uncertainty, latency tails, routing comparisons and swarm-ablation results. It returns a typed report and optional candidate policy table. Rust validates the result's schema, input identity, model/version, ranges and expiry before displaying or considering it. A Julia result cannot directly change a lease, grant permissions or dispatch a worker.

Start with file/stdio exchange for small data. Move larger arrays through a documented columnar/binary format only after measuring serialisation costs. Record shapes, dtypes, units, missing-value semantics and data ordering. Reject NaN, infinity, missing partitions and mismatched dataset IDs where a finite validated result is required. Use time/resource bounds and cancellation; a failed Julia analysis leaves the last approved routing baseline available.

Maintain one Julia `Project.toml`/`Manifest.toml` and reproducible inputs per release. Dependencies and compilation are prepared during packaging, not downloaded during an unattended task. Measure Julia cold start and precompilation; use a warm worker or sysimage only if the workload warrants the extra lifecycle. Do not embed Julia inside the Rust coordinator initially: a process boundary gives a clearer fault and memory boundary with less native-runtime coupling.

Language diversity alone does not create independent verification. If Rust and Julia implement the same mistaken formula or consume the same biased labels, they can agree and both be wrong. Use reference fixtures, deliberately corrupted inputs and task outcomes independent of the proposed scoring policy. Julia's analytical report should include missingness and selection effects, not just a point score.

### PyTorch options within a Rust and Julia codebase

| Path | What it provides | Cost/constraint | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Julia-native modelling with Lux / NeuralOperators.jl | Numerical research and operator models in the required language | Qualify selected accelerator, package versions and model operations | First choice for a Julia-owned experiment |
| Dedicated Rust worker using `tch` / LibTorch | PyTorch tensor operations through Rust bindings | Native library/version/device coupling and potentially large runtime | Evaluate when a PyTorch-compatible model or kernel is needed |
| Existing externally packaged PyTorch model service | Access to a maintained upstream model implementation | Another deployed dependency; may contain upstream Python | Optional service adapter, not a Python coordinator or new Python product code |
| Exported PyTorch model runtime | Potential deployment without the training environment | Export/operator/shape/runtime compatibility must be tested | Consider after a model proves useful; do not assume automatic interchange |

The `tch` project provides Rust bindings to the PyTorch C++ API; that does not make every Python neural-operator implementation callable without adaptation. Isolate it in a numerical worker rather than linking a large GPU runtime into the task coordinator. Pin and test the actual LibTorch/binding pair. [tch-rs](https://github.com/LaurentMazare/tch-rs).

PyTorch now deprecates TorchScript in favour of newer export/deployment paths. Do not base a new long-term plan on an assumed `torch.jit` workflow just because older Rust examples use it. Its limited stable ABI supports specific extension use cases; it is not a promise that arbitrary models, custom operators and every runtime binding interoperate. [PyTorch deprecation guidance](https://pytorch.org/blog/pytorch-2-12-release-blog/), [LibTorch ABI scope](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/libtorch_stable_abi.html).

### Where neural operators could be useful

A neural operator learns a mapping between functions or fields, unlike a conventional classifier that maps a fixed feature vector to a label. SciML's Julia library provides FNO, DeepONet and NOMAD architectures; the PyTorch NeuralOperator project provides an alternative implementation ecosystem. Neither is evidence that a neural operator improves LLM routing. [NeuralOperators.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/NeuralOperators/stable/), [NeuralOperator](https://neuraloperator.github.io/dev/).

Candidate uses are: predicting resource/latency fields from workload histories across time and worker topology; approximating an expensive coordination simulation used for offline scheduling experiments; or serving genuine scientific operator tasks requested by Habitat users. These are hypotheses to evaluate. Choosing among a few LLM recipes from sparse task metadata usually warrants rules, a small statistical model or a contextual policy first.

For a resource predictor, specify an input field of arrivals, resource pressure and queue state on a defined time/grid or graph domain, and an output field of latency/pressure over a declared horizon. Include masks for missing nodes and distinguish changing topology from missing telemetry. FNO's regular-grid/spectral assumptions may be inappropriate for a changing agent graph; consider a graph-aware model or a simpler baseline. Resolution transfer must be tested across the actual domains; it is not unlimited extrapolation.

The first experiment compares the candidate with persistence/last-value prediction, a simple statistical predictor and the existing rule policy. Hold out later time windows, task classes and at least one relevant topology/scale condition; report uncertainty and out-of-domain failure. Measure total training, data preparation, inference, memory and accelerator cost, including cold starts and data movement. A more accurate predictor with no useful scheduling gain is not sufficient.

A numerical service roster entry must name artifact/version, domain, input/output units and shapes, supported devices, validity limits, calibration/evaluation data and fallback. Promotion proceeds from offline evaluation to shadow prediction and then a bounded advisory use. Hard privacy, spend and ownership constraints remain in Rust. A learned model never controls unrestricted fan-out or writes its own success criteria.

sections.title: Token economy and complexity limits
sections.body:
Token cost is a product metric. The review did not have a reconciled invoice or token ledger for HEE-v2, so it does not invent a historical burn total. The user's experience of excessive cost is accepted as a design constraint. The changes below attack identifiable sources of waste.

| Cost source | Initial control | What to measure |
|---|---|---|
| LLM polling and status narration | Event-driven code; deduplicate and batch actionable notices | Model calls during idle/unchanged state; target zero |
| Routing every task through a large model | Explicit task profiles and local rules | Routing tokens and latency; default zero |
| Large repeated context | Task-scoped files, short handoff, cached stable prefix where supported | Input tokens and cache hits per accepted task |
| Repeated retries | One retry owner, original task ceiling, classify errors | Attempts and total cost including failures |
| Recursive delegation/review | Default one worker; bounded additional workers for a named benefit | Marginal cost and acceptance improvement |
| Repeated compaction | Record compaction usage; prefer fresh bounded tasks when appropriate | Compaction cost and lost-context failures |
| Too many documentation projections | One plan/atlas source and concise task context | Files read/changed per ordinary feature |
| Rebuilding solved infrastructure | Reuse worker runtimes, SQLite and systemd | Owned code and ongoing dependency burden |

Reserve spend before work. Estimate uncached/cached input, output/reasoning and expected retry/verification work separately; keep price timestamps and currency. Reconcile provider-reported usage afterward. Native subscription harnesses may expose incomplete per-task costs; mark those unknown or estimated instead of fabricating a zero marginal price. Hidden tool or compaction calls must not disappear from totals.

An absolute money ceiling cannot be enforced precisely when a chosen runtime does not expose or constrain its underlying calls. Such an adapter must declare an estimated-budget mode or remain ineligible for tasks demanding a hard provider-spend ceiling. Token/time/attempt bounds still apply. Provider limits and gateway budgets are useful backstops, not a substitute for whole-task accounting.

Initial complexity commitments: one coordinator service, one ledger, one retry owner per attempt, one task acceptance path, and no always-on LLM supervisor. The first release needs two worker types to demonstrate the abstraction, not ten adapters. A new crate, daemon, database, protocol or learned policy needs a named current consumer and a concrete reduction in failure or cost. These are architectural defaults, not a new bureaucracy of per-line approval.

Keep a compact developer entry point, one source of task status and narrowly scoped validation. Ordinary fixes should run relevant tests plus normal project checks. Independent review and fault drills focus on task ownership, budget enforcement, cancellation, secrets and release recovery. Do not require a complete adversarial research programme to change display text.

Avoid keeping broad synthetic cognition in the minimum product: no autonomous skill synthesis, workflow evolution, unvalidated neural control, cross-host consensus, multi-agent debate by default or custom cryptographic journal. Julia analysis is part of the design; PyTorch and neural operators have a defined evaluation lane below. Reintroduce a component only after a measured bottleneck identifies its value. Existing research remains available as a reference library.

sections.title: Fedora deployment atlas and trust boundaries
sections.body:
The first deployment target is this single Fedora Kinoite workstation. Host deployment and Toolbx development are separate environments. Build and check a reproducible release artifact with pinned dependencies; install only the resulting executable/configuration and explicitly selected worker runtime. Do not make a running development shell responsible for the service.

| Deployable | Placement / owner | State and interface | Failure action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coordinator | User systemd service; versioned release directory | Private runtime socket; XDG state database | Stop new admissions, recover ledger, expose reason |
| CLI / Herdr action | One-shot client | Calls coordinator; displays task result | Report unavailable; do not start a second scheduler |
| Pi worker | Pinned subprocess in an owned scope/container | JSONL pipes; private per-attempt session/workspace | Abort then bounded termination; retain artifacts |
| Native harness worker | Version-specific adapter in owned scope/container | Documented structured interface where available | Same attempt/recovery rules; no text-based success inference |
| Julia analysis | Pinned project invoked on demand in an owned process | Immutable datasets in; validated report/policy candidate out | Bound time/memory; retain approved baseline on failure |
| Optional numerical worker | Julia-native or isolated Rust/LibTorch process | Explicit domain/device/model contract | Reject incompatible or out-of-domain work; recorded fallback |
| Optional gateway | Separate explicitly configured service | Private endpoint; credentials isolated from task context | Ineligible route/circuit open; constrained fallback |
| Managed model/server service | Existing systemd unit or rootless Quadlet | Registered readiness and useful probe | Owner restart policy; no uncontrolled restart loop |
| SQLite and artifacts | User state directory on local filesystem | Coordinator owns writes; backups include artifact references | Stop writes on storage failure; disposable restore procedure |

Podman Quadlet integrates rootless containers with systemd user units and supports ordinary systemd dependency/resource options. Use it where container packaging is useful; do not containerise an in-process library merely to make the roster uniform. Confirm local cgroup/runtime behaviour and startup deadlines during commissioning. [Official Quadlet documentation](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-systemd.unit.5.html).

Keep the local control endpoint private to trusted operator clients. Peer UID checks and restrictive directory/socket permissions are a practical starting boundary, but all same-UID processes are not independent security principals. Worker containers must not receive the coordinator socket, ledger, broad home mounts or reusable provider credential stores. Tool permissions must be enforced outside an untrusted model's textual instructions. For hostile workloads or stronger isolation, qualify a dedicated user or VM boundary before expanding the trust claim.

Launch commands as argv with an explicit environment and working directory. Repository instructions and tool outputs are data, not permission to change task scope or credentials. A worktree prevents ordinary branch collisions; it is not a security sandbox. A trusted operator may deliberately run a native harness on the host, but that mode must be visible and not described as isolated execution.

The service roster distinguishes liveness, readiness and useful progress. Use bounded probes that exercise the real request path, monitor queue age and cancellation responsiveness, and keep unknown/stale states visible. An auxiliary heartbeat thread alone would not have caught ORAC's starvation incident. Alert on transitions and persistent actionable failure rather than feeding every probe to an LLM.

Operational records default to IDs, timings, counts and short reasons. Store prompts and tool outputs only according to the task's retention/privacy policy; redact credentials at ingestion and export. Retention must bound disk use without deleting the only evidence of an unresolved attempt. Optional standard telemetry can be added behind an export adapter; a monitoring platform is not required for launch.

Update by draining new work, finishing or checkpointing active attempts, backing up state, switching the release, and verifying a known small task. Revert the binary only when the prior version can read the schema; otherwise use a tested restore path. Service start, restart after login/reboot, low disk, provider outage, corrupt input and lost completion are commissioning cases. Remote fleets are a later extension, not part of the first release.

Core Rust modules share the binary release. External runtimes and integration packages have explicit compatible version ranges and immutable admitted versions per attempt; independent update does not mean arbitrary hot replacement. A restore changes the ledger epoch or forces event-client resynchronisation. See the schematic compatibility and rollout map.

sections.title: Full-stack quality and code-hardening contract
sections.body:
Hardening accompanies every implementation slice. The quality thread owns a small required-check manifest introduced in Phase 1; implementers run relevant checks, and integration verifies the combined candidate. Phase 5 broadens this to the supported release environment. No existing project checks are executed by this planning document.

| Surface | Required evidence | Important failure cases |
|---|---|---|
| Rust | Pinned compiler/Clippy/rustfmt; formatting; compiler warnings and pedantic Clippy; unit/integration/documentation tests | Blanket lint suppression, omitted supported features, zero discovered tests, swallowed exit status |
| Julia | Pinned Julia/project/manifest; formatter check; reproducible package tests; explicit bounds checks; numerical references | Dependency re-resolution, wrong units/order, silent precision loss, nonfinite results, stale datasets |
| Cross-language seam | Rust inputs consumed by Julia and Julia outputs checked by Rust against independently specified expectations | Unsupported schema, missing partitions, precision/overflow, truncated/oversized records, mismatched identities |
| Shared state and recovery | Reference state model, bounded event-sequence tests and disposable real-process failures | Concurrent reservations, cancel/accept race, late verifier, restart between commit and delivery |
| Worker / service adapters | Contract fixtures plus permitted real-runtime checks on supported versions | Mock-only success, model identity mismatch, incomplete cancellation, stalled useful-health path |
| Verification instrument | Protected mandatory fixtures, exact subject/check identity, status and executed/skipped case counts | Worker-edited acceptance, wrong tree, missing report, unexpected zero-test run, broken checker treated as pass |
| Packaged full stack | Source/dependency/toolchain identity, shipped digest, install/readback, end-to-end loop and restore/rollback | Testing a different build, runtime dependency downloads, stale deployed configuration, incompatible rollback |

The initial Rust command contract should include `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings -D clippy::pedantic`, and the applicable locked unit/integration/doc test invocations. These are proposed recipes to qualify against the selected project/toolchain, not commands to execute now. Check each supported feature configuration; `--all-features` alone does not exercise distinct combinations. If tests use `--all-targets`, retain a separate documentation-test path because that selection excludes doctests. Enable applicable restriction lints individually. Permit narrowly scoped exceptions with a recorded engineering reason; never blanket-disable pedantic checks to obtain a green build. [Clippy usage](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/clippy/usage.html), [Cargo test targets](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-test.html), [feature configurations](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html).

Julia's gate uses a selected formatter in check mode, the locked test environment with `Pkg.test(allow_reresolve=false)`, and explicitly enabled `--check-bounds=yes` for the test process. Current Pkg documentation states that tests inherit the parent bounds mode; do not rely on an assumed default. Pin development-check tools separately from runtime needs. Add further static analysis only when it addresses a named gap. Numerical tolerances must follow the domain/reference error, not whatever makes a failing test pass. [Pkg test contract](https://pkgdocs.julialang.org/v1/api/), [JuliaFormatter](https://github.com/JuliaEditorSupport/JuliaFormatter.jl).

Use the Rust–Julia contract corpus in both directions. Identity fields require exact preservation; numerical outputs use declared tolerances. A round trip implemented by one side alone is insufficient. The fixture set includes schema/version/unknown-field policy, integer range and precision, array order/shape/units, missingness, finite-value requirements, malformed framing and stale dataset IDs. Keep fixtures independent of the candidate scoring algorithm.

For ownership, budgets and acceptance, compare bounded event schedules with a small sequential reference model. Retain a seed or event schedule for reproduction. Supplement this with actual disposable process termination/restart at the documented transaction boundaries. Use targeted fuzzing/property tests for parsers and state transitions. Add Miri or sanitizers when unsafe/FFI or a specific memory concern warrants them; these tools do not prove the whole product safe, and need not become mandatory for every display edit.

The coordinator launches named verifier recipes whose acceptance policy and mandatory fixtures are outside worker write authority. Worker-authored tests are additional evidence. Capture the exact subject, command/recipe, checker version, exit status, discovered/executed/skipped cases and decisive output. Unexpected zero-test execution, missing reports and skipped mandatory criteria are verification errors. A deliberately failing fixture must demonstrate that the instrument detects the intended fault; deeper mutation testing focuses on consequential logic.

Release checks run against the packaged candidate through `submit → route → worker → verify/repair → ledger → Julia report → Herdr view → completion delivery`, including a service useful-health failure and backup/restore/rollback. Record which steps used a real runtime and which used fixtures. Individual thread completion and a large test count cannot replace this integrated observation. Keep check results in the completion evidence manifest so future agents can see what actually passed without reloading the whole research corpus.

Gate qualification requires a valid unmutated baseline and an independently justified intended fault. Preserve invalid-fixture, excluded and unmeasured outcomes. A formatting failure that masks the intended behavioral defect is not evidence for the behavioral detector; use benign near-neighbors where false positives matter. Non-blocking authoring hooks are feedback and cannot replace an availability-aware enforced release check. These lessons from the [Toolshed gate review](evidence/toolshed-final-context.md) extend T25/T17/T27, without a new universal test matrix.

### Candidate execution inside verification

The trusted launcher and evidence collector remain outside candidate-controlled execution. Compilers may execute build scripts and procedural macros; test binaries and Julia package hooks also execute candidate code. Those subprocesses receive the qualified execution boundary and cannot write protected fixtures, authoritative evidence, coordinator ledger/socket or unrelated secrets. The collector records actual process observations; structured reports produced by candidate code remain claims checked against the frozen recipe and independent expectations. Capturing exit status does not prove arbitrary report truth. Before T15 qualifies stronger isolation, trusted-host verification must explicitly report its weaker containment scope.

sections.title: Security hardening and the Codex security thread
sections.body:
The dedicated security profile is **Daybreak Blue (`gpt-daybreak-blue-latest`)**, confirmed in the local Codex model cache and available delegation interface during this review. A bounded planning-review thread was launched with that model. The official description identifies a defensive cybersecurity model alias and notes separate access provisioning. Session availability does not establish future API availability, immutable underlying identity or a permanent model choice; record effective model/version when exposed. Model specialisation is useful expertise, not authority to bypass task limits. [Official model documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-daybreak-blue-latest).

Use the security thread for an initial threat model, change-focused reviews of sensitive boundaries, reproducible defensive findings and re-verification after fixes. Codex Security's documented hardening workflow is a future integration option; this review did not install the plugin, run a scan or establish plugin provisioning. Keep the engine's security profile behind the same replaceable worker contract. [Codex Security hardening](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/security/plugin/security-hardening).

| Boundary | Required design and acceptance case |
|---|---|
| Task authority vs untrusted content | Coordinator-owned task policy controls paths, egress, secrets, service actions and acceptance changes. Label source/provenance in context. Malicious repository/tool text cannot widen authority or weaken a criterion. Tool requests are checked outside the model. |
| Operator IPC vs workers | Private 0700 runtime directory, peer checks, method-level authorisation and bounded requests. Workers receive neither the control socket nor its credentials. Test read-only versus mutation permissions. Same-UID host workers remain a trusted mode; stronger separation needs a dedicated UID or VM boundary. |
| Credentials | Deliver only the selected attempt's needed credential using a compatible credential file/service facility; scrub inherited environment and tool-child context. Never put secrets in argv, prompts, receipts or roster exports. If a harness requires environment/home credentials, document exposure and restrict its supported trust profile. |
| Process, path and stream inputs | Resolve intended executable identity and launch typed argv without implicit shell interpolation. An explicitly allowed shell tool remains inside the task's enforced filesystem/network boundary. Bound record depth/size, output, backpressure and request identities. Validate artifact type and descriptor-relative containment; reject symlink/rename escapes and special-file substitution. |
| Old generations and integration | Separate writable attempt workspaces; no reassignment into a still-active writer's tree. Terminate or quarantine before reuse. Only selected candidates enter integration; stale callbacks and external-effect ambiguity cannot be hidden by an expired lease. |
| Verifier and evidence origin | Coordinator launches a protected checker and captures its actual observations. A worker-supplied pass-shaped JSON, changed fixture, wrong subject or same-model agreement cannot create trusted passing evidence. |
| Dependencies and release | Lock Cargo/Julia dependencies and selected worker/runtime versions; record container digests, provenance and licences. Separate explicit dependency acquisition from a network-disabled build. Detect installed binary/unit/config drift before accepting the deployment claim. |
| Resource and state integrity | Bound CPU, memory, PIDs, wall time, messages, artifacts and disk retention for workers and verifiers. Restrict state paths, validate artifact metadata/content and test disk-full/WAL/corruption/output-flood cases without false acceptance or loss of unresolved evidence. |

Secret-file deletion does not revoke a copied provider token. Use provider expiry/revocation where available and record what can actually be invalidated. A process that must call a provider necessarily has some credential authority; isolate untrusted tool execution from that authority or admit the weaker trust mode. No promised secret-containment property is closed until it is tested on the actual harness and host boundary. Avoid inventing a new credential broker unless the selected runtime needs one.

The security finding record stays compact: affected source/build, threat prerequisite, reproducible observation, impact, proposed fix, owner, status, verification reference and accepted residual limitation. A severity label is not proof. Distinguish a confirmed defect, unconfirmed concern, hardening improvement and accepted limitation. The security model cannot unilaterally waive a mandatory criterion. Release requires closure or explicit disposition of material findings under the agreed release contract, with regression evidence for fixes.

The review is scoped to the declared workstation deployment and authorised disposable fixtures. Existing same-UID processes and host compromise limit what socket permissions and checksums can guarantee. Source inspection, lint success and a security model's opinion do not establish runtime containment. A dedicated model review can find different errors, but this plan makes no formal independent assurance claim.

### Candidate execution inside verification

The trusted launcher and evidence collector remain outside candidate-controlled execution. Compilers may execute build scripts and procedural macros; test binaries and Julia package hooks also execute candidate code. Those subprocesses receive the qualified execution boundary and cannot write protected fixtures, authoritative evidence, coordinator ledger/socket or unrelated secrets. The collector records actual process observations; structured reports produced by candidate code remain claims checked against the frozen recipe and independent expectations. Capturing exit status does not prove arbitrary report truth. Before T15 qualifies stronger isolation, trusted-host verification must explicitly report its weaker containment scope.

sections.title: Top-tail performance through evidence and synthetic-coder lessons
sections.body:
The user's top-7% direction is treated as an ambition for architectural quality and outcomes. It is not an established percentile. A credible percentile needs a named reference population, comparable tasks, a scoring rule and measured uncertainty. “Top 7% in every field” cannot be established by one aggregate benchmark or by assigning the system a self-rated score.

Translate the ambition into a demanding evaluation programme: accepted output quality, total task cost, turnaround, reliability, security-boundary behaviour, recoverability and operator workload. Report per task class and adverse condition. Include p50/p95 latency and failure tails where the sample supports them; do not hide a weak class inside the mean. Compare with a strong single-worker baseline as well as the current swarm. If there is no credible public comparison set, report local improvement rather than a percentile.

The original synthetic-coder records provide concrete lessons. One ORAC review propagated a wrong enum count because a regex could not match digits in `A2aTask`; a worker reading the actual source caught it. A separate verifier account lists wrong-tree checks, stale identity records, inferred signatures, fixture faults and suppressed counter-evidence. These records support a method, not a claim that the old system achieved a percentile. [ORAC reconciliation](sources/S20.md), [instrument failures](sources/S05.md).

| Failure pattern | Design/process response | Evidence expected |
|---|---|---|
| Fluent claims about files that do not exist | Resolve every critical implementation claim to the actual source before planning an import | Source path and bounded dependency closure |
| Tests aimed at the wrong tree or stale build | Bind important checks to the candidate and environment actually used | Build/config identity and decisive observations |
| A broken verifier mistaken for a product bug | Validate fixture/interface first; preserve refuting evidence | A control that reaches the intended boundary |
| Endpoints healthy but consumers unwired | Exercise producer → transport → consumer → accepted result | Correlated event/artifact path, not endpoint counts |
| Agent agreement mistaken for correctness | Independent initial evidence, explicit dissent and artifact checks | Errors found beyond shared model judgment |
| “Done” from output, score or generation exhaustion | Separate worker completion, evaluation validity and task acceptance | Negative exit, malformed score and stale result tests |
| Increasing activity mistaken for progress | Measure accepted output and marginal cohort value | Swarm ablations including total tokens and human rework |

Use proportionate verification. The way to avoid expensive assurance theatre is to target the real failure boundary and stop redundant rechecking after the required checks pass, unless the subject or concern changes. A release-level recovery check is valuable; copying dozens of status projections after every edit is not automatically valuable. Preserve evidence needed for review without requiring future agents to reload the entire historical corpus.

The architectural standard is selective strength: a small operational core, a useful Julia analysis lane, explicit worker/service ownership, and optional learned components whose gains survive controlled comparison. If a stronger alternative reduces complexity while meeting the same outcomes, change the plan and record the evidence for that decision.

sections.title: Vision alignment, capacity and gap analysis
sections.body:
### Does this iteration align with the vision?

**At the planning level, yes:** the atlas covers supported-model routing, task-specific selection, agent/service rosters, Rust/Julia modules, bounded specialist threads, verification loops, security, API/socket ownership and discoverable LLM tools. It deliberately treats HEE-v2 as a component source and makes numerical control conditional on measured benefit. The user-requirement trace exposes that alignment.

**At the executable level, alignment is not yet demonstrated:** v3 has not been implemented. This iteration offers a source-backed architectural proposal, module/transport maps, a task graph and acceptance contracts. It does not yet offer a running engine, tested routing policy, enforced budget, persistent thread roster or proof-of-completion service. The available Herdr server and source components are valuable foundations; their existence cannot close v3's system-level claims.

| Capacity / feature | Current evidenced position | Needed to claim v3 capacity |
|---|---|---|
| Route local/remote models | Pi/provider and native-harness interfaces researched; no v3 adapter runs | Two qualified adapters, effective identity, capability refusals and a real task |
| Select the best supported recipe | Policies and evaluation method designed; no Habitat comparison result | Baseline/held-out outcomes, whole-task costs and uncertainty by task class |
| Agent/service/thread roster | Several source registries and historical mechanisms inspected | One v3 authority with current observations, lifecycle rules and restart recovery |
| Closed execute/verify/repair loop | Historical failure evidence and proposed closure predicate | An actual failed candidate repaired to acceptance; exhaustion and checker failure stop truthfully |
| Synergistic specialist work | Three bounded planning reviews occurred in this Codex session | Durable engine thread/mailbox/ownership and parent-integration behaviour; session reviews are not that runtime |
| Julia / neural capacity | Statistical and numerical contracts specified | Reproducible Julia reports; optional operator experiments must establish domain and useful benefit |
| API/socket and LLM tools | Herdr status/schema observed; v3 interfaces/catalogue proposed | Schema-consistent CLI/API/tool implementation with enforced caller scope and result readback |
| Bash / Pi / skills / chaining | Selected vault and pinned upstream contracts reviewed; no v3 integrations installed | T29 qualifies thin versioned packages, two real compositions and safe updates |
| Hardened deployment | Threat/check/release contracts specified | Actual packaged full-stack tests, finding dispositions, restore/rollback and real-work pilot |

### Is it scalable?

The planned scope is one workstation. It can be designed to handle more queued tasks, bounded concurrent workers and additional adapters without multiplying coordinator services. This is an architectural provision, not a throughput benchmark. Admission must account for CPU, RAM, GPU/VRAM when present, provider quotas and budget. Unknown capacity must remain unknown; host RAM alone cannot determine local-model feasibility.

One SQLite writer and one coordinator deliberately limit operational complexity. Bound event frequency, message queues and artifact retention; keep token-stream payloads out of the task ledger. Use indexed task/roster queries, backpressure and explicit overload rejection. Keep blocking filesystem/database work from starving runtime cancellation and health paths. Measure sustained task/event rate, queue delay, transaction latency, cancellation latency, memory, disk growth and Julia cold start before claiming capacity or tuning concurrency.

Multi-host execution, failover and high availability are not current release features. Their introduction would require a concrete distributed identity/lease/resource model and failure tests, rather than merely replacing the socket with TCP. Keep interfaces capable of an adapter extension, but do not import a cluster database or consensus service ahead of a measured need. Recovery from one coordinator failure is a first-release obligation; uninterrupted service during host failure is not yet promised.

### Is it maintainable?

The planned boundaries favour maintainability: cohesive private modules, one source for action/schema projections, one task-state writer, existing runtime/lifecycle owners, documented forward/return contracts and a compact operator entry point. Those choices must be tested through real changes. Observe change propagation, defect recurrence, time to diagnose/repair, test reliability and dependency-upgrade burden. A large diagram or small file count is not evidence of maintainability by itself.

The main risk is reintroducing a second framework through the atlas: too many empty modules, one service per responsibility, copied status projections, a universal plugin system or a mandatory review swarm. Keep this comprehensive research bundle as a reference, while each coding task receives only its contract, affected interfaces, evidence and required checks. Consolidation updates the same task/atlas records; it does not require every future agent to reread the whole corpus.

### Conventional gap analysis

| Priority | Gap | Recommendation / closure |
|---|---|---|
| First slice | No v3 executable proves the core seam | T01/T25/T26 define task, quality and threat contracts; T02/T03 qualify the small worker interface, then T06 closes one loop |
| First slice | Source/package compatibility is untested | Pin actual Rust/Julia/Pi/native versions and test framing, effective model, cancellation and accounting limits |
| Foundation | Durability, concurrency and false completion remain design properties | T04/T07/T17 exercise state transactions, stale effects, verifier errors and recovery with real disposable processes |
| Foundation | Owned API/LLM surfaces could drift or overgrant | T28 derives them from one action catalogue and checks equivalent denial/effects across transports |
| Measured routing | No trustworthy local quality/cost leaderboard | T12/T21 collect complete outcomes, including failures and rework; retain simple profiles until improvement is supported |
| Habitat operation | Roster observations and host boundaries are not qualified | T13–T16 test useful health, explicit lifecycle ownership, actual user/container isolation and Herdr reconciliation |
| Release | No packaged end-to-end or security closure exists | T18/T27/T19 verify the shipped candidate, material findings, restore/rollback and the declared pilot |
| Optional research | Neural operators and coupling have no demonstrated routing/cohesion gain | T23/T24 use domain-specific held-out tests and simple baselines; reject added machinery when benefit is absent |

### Non-anthropocentric gap analysis

Here this means evaluating the system as interacting processes, state machines, data and physical resources. Terms such as “agent,” “cohesion” and “confidence” are useful labels, but they do not establish cognition, agreement with reality or useful control. Human intent and authorisation still define the objective and permitted effects.

| Machine property | Gap / misleading proxy | Engineering response and evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Closed causal paths | A producer emits, but no intended consumer acts; endpoint-up hides a disconnected return path | Trace task/attempt/event identity through dispatch, verification, acceptance and delivery; inject a missing consumer and detect the unresolved obligation |
| Exclusive effect ownership | Lease state changes while an old process can still write | Separate writable generations; terminate/quarantine; integrate only selected immutable candidates; measure stale-effect rejection |
| Information integrity | Shared context is large but stale, unbound or contradictory | Versioned briefs, provenance, bounded relevant deltas and preserved dissent; check obsolete-message and candidate-identity failures |
| Resource feasibility | Busy workers and high token throughput appear productive | Admission/backpressure based on actual resources, total cost and accepted output; idle makes zero model calls |
| Valid feedback | A model's score or oscillator synchrony substitutes for task correctness | Protected acceptance criteria and independent reference fixtures; test whether numerical signals predict real errors before using them |
| Observability | PID/heartbeat is alive while the useful request path stalls | Bounded useful probes, queue/cancellation latency and end-to-end event consumption; reproduce starvation and slow-consumer cases |
| Control stability | Retry, supervisor, gateway and cohort loops amplify one another | One retry owner, original budget, explicit no-progress rule and bounded fan-out; test repeated failures and outage recovery |
| Distribution and domain validity | A learned policy or operator extrapolates beyond its evidence | Hold out time/task/topology domains, report uncertainty and out-of-domain refusals; preserve a validated fallback |
| Evidence custody | Schema-valid pass records are accepted regardless of origin | Protected checker launch and fixture identity; capture observations outside worker write authority; reject forged, missing and wrong-subject evidence |
| Failure containment | One output flood, memory exhaustion or corrupt store spreads across the habitat | Process/resource boundaries, storage limits and truthful unknown state; retain recoverable evidence and stop admissions when needed |

### Recommendations and review cadence

Keep the new composition architecture and mandatory Rust/Julia split. Preserve simple deterministic control and use specialist reasoning only for tasks that need it. Put the execute–verify–repair path, protected evidence, initial lint/test contract and threat model into the first useful slice. Build rosters, context/thread coherence and the action catalogue around that path rather than as independent frameworks.

Measure routing quality and whole-task economy before adding learned selection. Treat API portability, modularity and a future worker adapter as extension points, not evidence of multi-host scale. Defer optional neural control, mandatory gateways and additional daemons until their benefit survives a controlled comparison. Use the security model to find and challenge weaknesses, with actual test evidence closing findings.

Revisit vision alignment after each accepted vertical slice, a material interface/authority change, or evidence of cost/reliability drift. Ask what executable capacity exists, which claim its evidence supports, how a real change propagated, which resource limits were measured and which gap remains. Update the same requirement/task/module records. Do not turn this into periodic LLM polling or a new approval ceremony. If a smaller or stronger design meets the same objective with better evidence, supersede the affected decision and change the plan.

sections.title: Delivery sequence and production acceptance
sections.body:
Deliver vertical slices that can be used and evaluated. The task graph below has 29 proposed tasks: five delivery phases and a separate optional numerical research phase. Its dependencies are engineering prerequisites, not calendar promises. There is no justified duration estimate until the first adapter slice establishes implementation effort.

**Phase 1 — Prove the small seam.** Freeze a short task contract, choose the initial worker/version pair, and demonstrate submit/model readback/usage/settled completion/cancel with fixtures. Confirm the Rust/Pi interface and Julia data contract from that seam. Produce a tiny executable path before expanding the architecture.

**Phase 2 — Own work durably.** Add SQLite, task attempts and leases; register agents/models; build one end-to-end task path with result checking and restart reconciliation. The milestone is one contained development task whose outcome and cost remain intelligible after a forced coordinator restart.

**Phase 3 — Route economically.** Add the second adapter, strict eligibility, declared cost mode, bounded fallback, scoped context and a small comparative task suite. The milestone is a defensible choice between two recipes, with effective model readback and total task cost. A simple policy is allowed to win.

**Phase 4 — Operate the habitat.** Add inspect-only service inventory, useful probes, selected systemd lifecycle actions, worker isolation and the Herdr task view. The milestone is an operator who can see, cancel and recover work without asking a model to interpret raw logs.

**Phase 5 — Qualify and release.** Run ownership/budget/recovery fault cases, packaging/backup/rollback checks and a constrained real-work pilot. Complete an operator runbook and a concise release record. Expand task classes and services only after the pilot's failures are understood.

Production acceptance for the declared workstation scope requires:

- Both worker adapters pass their documented launch, effective-model, streaming, usage, completion and cancellation cases. Unsupported operations are explicit.
- Concurrent submission and crash recovery do not assign two live write owners to the same attempt/workspace. Stale results are rejected.
- Acceptance checks run against the actual resulting artifact; an end event or exit zero alone cannot accept a task.
- Budgets include routing, retries and checking, with unknown accounting visible. Fallback cannot change privacy or capabilities silently.
- A service's stale or failed useful probe cannot be displayed as healthy; lifecycle changes have an identified owner.
- Backup/restore and version rollback work on disposable state. Storage errors stop further writes without disguising incomplete work.
- No model requests occur during a controlled idle interval. The interval and observed calls are recorded, not inferred from configuration.
- The pilot records accepted/failed tasks, cost per accepted task, turnaround, operator rework and unresolved incidents. Latency/resource targets are set from measured workstation capacity before release, not invented by this report.

The old HEE G1 requirement for 30 days of collector data remains an obligation for that programme if it continues. It is not silently inherited as a launch prerequisite for this smaller engine. The new release contract must explicitly define its pilot workload, observation window and acceptable error rates in Phase 1 and confirm them in Phase 5.

The first authorised coding task, when implementation is requested, should be the small adapter slice and task contract. Do not start by generating every proposed module, importing all 46 HEE packets, or writing a new architecture corpus.

sections.title: Open choices, risks and how to extend this plan
sections.body:
The default design is settled enough to build a reviewable first slice, while a few choices need evidence. The decision ledger distinguishes reversible defaults from future commissioning decisions. None is a request for confirmation now.

The main uncertainties are worker-version compatibility, actual available provider accounts, native harness accounting, GPU capacity, the amount of reusable code whose dependency closure stays small, and the local workload that defines model quality. Source inspection resolves architecture questions but cannot measure these outcomes. The plan avoids selecting a current “best model” without tasks and results.

The primary implementation risk is turning the coordinator into a replacement for every existing tool. Keep ownership narrow: task scheduling/accounting/rosters, adapter contracts and operator visibility. Another risk is simplifying away essential recovery. Transactions, generations, cancellation and truthful unknown states are small mechanisms with direct value; they belong in the initial product.

Reuse should occur at the smallest coherent boundary. For each proposed import, record the upstream revision, licence/attribution, dependency closure, local consumer and behaviour tested. Prefer a maintained package for the provider/agent loop and a small local module for policy. Do not copy legacy code into an existing cleanroom tree against that tree's rules. This proposal targets a separate small composition project; the original projects are left unchanged.

The roadmap is independent of HEE's existing canonical identifiers. Links to its 46-packet index remain for provenance and optional later reuse, not as a second hidden backlog. If a component is later adopted, map that specific component and its useful tests into the new task. Preserve the old records without making their process mandatory. [Historical packet index](sources/C22.json).

Maintain one JSON planning spine, its Markdown report and the generated offline HTML atlas. Keep source snapshots and receipts beside them. To broaden the vision, add a real use case, identify which existing port cannot support it, and change that boundary only. An extension should earn its place through a smaller workload cost, a new necessary capability or a demonstrated reliability improvement.

### Current user-requirement trace

Coverage means the planning requirement is represented, not that the engine exists.

decisions.resolution: Revisit only for measured multi-host/write-throughput requirements.

tasks.acceptance: Fixture and later permitted smoke cases cover LF framing, model readback, usage, queued work, retry/end/settled ordering, cancellation and malformed/truncated records. Record the supported Rust/Pi protocol pair; no broad framework scaffold.

tasks.validation_cmd: Proposed, not implemented: habitat-engine-check case T03 --fixture-root <disposable-fixtures>
tasks.acceptance: Launch, observe, cancel and result semantics work for tool-capable and output-only models. Missing features return unsupported; normalisation retains provider-specific usage and actual identity.

tasks.intent: Establish the Rust and Julia quality contract
tasks.validation_cmd: Proposed, not implemented: habitat-engine-check case T25 --fixture-root <disposable-fixtures>
tasks.acceptance: Pinned format/lint/test recipes include pedantic Clippy, supported feature profiles, Rust doctests, locked Julia tests with explicit bounds checks, and honest case/skip counts. A deliberately bad fixture fails for the intended reason. Checks grow with each vertical slice; no blanket lint suppression. The verifier recipe separates trusted launch/collection from candidate-controlled compiler/build/test processes. Captured process exit status is an observation; candidate structured reports remain claims requiring recipe checks and independent expectations. Early trusted-host fixture tests must disclose that stronger hostile-code containment is not yet qualified. Qualify consequential gate discrimination on a passing baseline and an independently justified fault with the intended failure reason; include benign near-neighbors where false positives matter. Non-blocking authoring hooks do not satisfy required release gates.

tasks.intent: Define the threat model and security review contract
tasks.validation_cmd: Proposed, not implemented: habitat-engine-check case T26 --fixture-root <disposable-fixtures>
tasks.acceptance: Map task authority, context provenance, credentials, IPC, same-UID limits, isolation and trusted verifier ownership. Assign bounded negative cases and finding disposition. Confirm the selected security-model capability without granting extra execution authority. Include candidate-controlled build scripts, procedural macros, test binaries and Julia package hooks in the threat model; invoking them via a trusted verifier confers no collector authority.

tasks.intent: Implement the transactional task ledger
tasks.validation_cmd: Proposed, not implemented: habitat-engine-check case T04 --fixture-root <disposable-fixtures>
tasks.acceptance: Submission replay is idempotent; same key with different content conflicts; task/attempt/event updates commit together; migrations and consistent backup have failure tests. The first ledger includes atomic conservative work/verification reservations, effect uncertainty and cancellation intent. task.get can recover a lost admission reply by principal-scoped request key. Allocate event identity before immutable manifest creation; acceptance commits its reference with the outbox. Publish immutable artifacts crash-durably under a declared filesystem contract before committing their SQLite references; a completed write alone is insufficient. Use file/metadata synchronisation and atomic publication as required by that contract. Historical acceptance and current evidence availability are separate facts.

tasks.intent: Build the model and agent roster
tasks.validation_cmd: Proposed, not implemented: habitat-engine-check case T05 --fixture-root <disposable-fixtures>
tasks.acceptance: Profiles and instances are distinct; declared/effective capabilities and freshness are visible; disable prevents new work; importing a roster starts nothing; secrets remain references. SQLite owns admitted roster revisions. Reviewed TOML manifests are explicit bootstrap/import/export inputs through the same validated update authority: expected-absent creates, expected-revision updates. Invalid or stale import changes nothing. Test update/disable, restart and stale re-import; no admitted mutation is lost and disabled records remain disabled. Active attempts retain their pinned record snapshots.

tasks.intent: Close one execute–verify–repair loop with completion evidence
tasks.validation_cmd: Proposed, not implemented: habitat-engine-check case T06 --fixture-root <disposable-fixtures>
tasks.acceptance: A contained task uses the selected recipe and owned workspace, produces an artifact, runs an actual acceptance check and records result/cost. Worker end or exit zero alone cannot accept it. A failing candidate is repaired and reverified; exhausted and verifier-error cases stop truthfully. Acceptance and completion outbox event commit together with a criterion-to-evidence manifest bound to the actual candidate. Even this first loop requires a safe minimal budget gate and reserved verification allocation; unknown accounting cannot satisfy a hard ceiling. Rich cross-adapter reconciliation follows in T10. Terminal cancellation requires observed cleanup/effect reconciliation.

tasks.intent: Recover and cancel owned attempts
tasks.validation_cmd: Proposed, not implemented: habitat-engine-check case T07 --fixture-root <disposable-fixtures>
tasks.acceptance: Crashes before/after dispatch acknowledgement, stale generations, PID reuse, queued Pi messages and partial cleanup produce correct recoverable states without duplicate writes. Ambiguous external outcomes remain explicit. Cover restart at verification/evidence/acceptance boundaries; lease expiry alone cannot authorize reuse of a still-writable old workspace. Acceptance explicitly rejects any earlier committed cancellation intent, even before terminal cleanup. If acceptance committed first, later cancellation cannot rewrite history. Startup may reattach observation to a positively reconciled live attempt without redispatch. Restored ledger epochs cannot silently reuse prior event cursors.

tasks.intent: Implement the bounded Rust–Julia analysis exchange
tasks.validation_cmd: Proposed, not implemented: habitat-engine-check case T21 --fixture-root <disposable-fixtures>
tasks.acceptance: An immutable attempt dataset produces a reproducible Julia report with dataset/schema identity. Missing data, nonfinite values, stale results, timeout and cancellation are explicit. Julia failure preserves the approved route and cannot mutate task ownership. Exercise the bidirectional contract corpus with independent expectations, numeric tolerances and explicit Julia bounds checks.

tasks.validation_cmd: Proposed, not implemented: habitat-engine-check case T08 --fixture-root <disposable-fixtures>
tasks.acceptance: A selected native harness or plain inference backend passes the common contract; actual supported model/effort is recorded. No success inferred from terminal prose. Version-specific limitations are listed.
